home.greeting: Hello! My name is Sun. I'm a game programmer who deeply enjoys the journey of creating games. I built this website to serve as an archive of my experiences—feel free to look around!

profile.p1: Hello! If you have stumbled onto this page, I figure I owe you a proper introduction.
profile.p2: I'm Sunwoo Lee, I make games for a living. I find joy and fulfillment in the journey of creating games. I grew up playing all kinds of games — RPGs, platformers, strategy, party, shooters, etc — and still am an avid gamer. Although Steam is not the only platform for gaming, if you are interested in my gaming profile, you can find me
profile.p3: While I was going through my military service, I had an abundance of time to meditate and think about life since I had no phones or computers in my vicinity to distract me. I regularly meditated and reflected upon my past to analyze what I truly value in life. Since then, I stopped seeing games as just entertainment and started appreciating them for what they really are: a unique blend of storytelling, visuals, music, and interactivity that no other medium can pull off quite the same way. Naturally, I wanted to create such experiences myself.
profile.p4: Fast-forward to today, and I have a few years of professional experience under my belt, working across gameplay, tools, UI, animation, and more. I've put this website together to show what I've been up to — and to see where the road takes me next. Feel free to poke around!

climb.p1: C.L.I.M.B is an incremental 3D climbing game I am currently developing. My goal for this project is to learn how to create games using UE5 and C++.
climb.p2: Although the main objective of this project is to learn a new language and engine, I am enjoying having full authorship of the entire codebase and participating in the design of core gameplay mechanics.

mlp.p1: Working on My Little Puppy at Dreamotion was my first professional project and a massive leap from my student days. Collaborating with a team of up to 30 people taught me how to work within established pipelines, communicate with other team members with different roles (not just engineers), and deliver production quality work under tight deadlines. And by tight deadlines, I mean one to two days to complete entire features.
mlp.p2: Participating in the development and experiencing the full cycle of a game project until its release was quite an experience. Unlike the indie games I had worked on previously, creating a big commercial game made me realize the complexity and scale of such projects. Also, trying a 3D platformer gave me new insights as well as tough challenges in programming that I enjoyed solving.
mlp.p3: Shipping on multiple platforms gave me some insight into platform specific development that I wouldn't have experienced anywhere else. Towards the tail end of development, I had the opportunity to try out different fields of work (like DevOps, PM, Localizing, and Game Design) while porting the game to different platforms that I would have otherwise not experienced.
mlp.li2: Collaborate with others to implement 3Cs, specifically tuned for a 'dog-like' feel
mlp.li3: Collaborate with others to implement core system mechanics
mlp.li4: Implement event system that would be utilized throughout the entire game
mlp.li5: Implement in-game and out-game UI with art and design departments for gameplay systems and menu
mlp.li7: Collaborate with outsourced sound designers to implement audio solutions
mlp.t_li3: Built visual scripting tool for the core event system
mlp.p4: Early in the project, every narrative sequence was hard-coded, including repetitive tasks like triggering animations at certain timings. But as the project progressed, we realized that these tasks were becoming bottlenecks for the sequences that the designers had envisioned.
mlp.p5: Instead of programmers trying to figure out the details for that scene's narrative sequences, I built a system and an editor tool that gave designers (and everybody else) a way to author events themselves. This drastically sped up our creative process, enabling all members to test and iterate on multiple ideas without waiting on a programmer (AKA me).
mlp.p6: What started as a simple tool for narrative sequences quickly scaled into the core of our game's logic. We expanded Barista for use in cutscenes, trigger events, checkpoint progression, and more. Ultimately, it became an essential tool that enabled most scripted events in MLP, streamlining our entire development process.
mlp.p7: To support MLP's release across PC, PS5, and Nintendo Switch, I implemented an abstraction layer over Unity's Input System.
mlp.p8: The OmniInput class handles real-time device switching and key/pad remapping. It features a dynamic sprite mapper that translates raw inputs into platform-specific key sprites. This ensured console compliance and allowed designers to write text in Baristas without worrying about the active hardware. All the UIs (in-game, menu, settings, etc...) would be affected by this system.
mlp.p9: Bringing MLP to the Nintendo Switch, PS5, and LG TV introduced me and my fellow porting team member to strict hardware constraints that required aggressive optimization. Working with limited memory and specs gave me a newfound respect for older console games. Developers back in the days were using black magics to run games so seamlessly on limited hardwares...
mlp.p10: For the Nintendo Switch, I created a profiling system and helped optimize the base game, ensuring we maintained a stable framerate without sacrificing the game's visual aesthetic. (or at least, trying my best to preserve it) This was a great opportunity for me to learn all kinds of optimization techniques. For PS5, optimization was not an issue, but the TRC was a hassle to meet.
mlp.fig3: FPS graph on Switch generated through code & profiling
mlp.p11: Beyond raw performance, translating the game to console required tweaking values to improve player experience. We rebalanced the difficulty of mini-games, overhauled the input handling to smooth out the roughness of the controls, and added additional mechanics to assist platforming. The goal was to ensure the dog's movement and platforming feel natural and responsive on a thumbstick, providing a good experience across all devices.
mlp.p12: The difference in platforms caused a lot of issues in the game, so naturally, a quick cycle of testing and fixing was crucial. I utilized CI tools, including Jenkins, NintendoSDK, and PS5SDK, to automate our deployment processes. This allowed the team to run fast, on-device iterations and test sessions, helping catch TRC violations and bugs more conveniently. This automated process increased our overall development speed.

space.p1: This project was created for the Capstone Project of KRAFTON Jungle bootcamp.
space.p2: From a programming perspective, building this game gave me insights into how a client should be structured for a networked environment.
space.p3: As the project lead, I learned about the importance of collaboration and communication between team members, scheduling and task delegation, and how to effectively convey a game design vision to the other members. This project taught me what it takes to lead a team.
space.li3: UI input handling, animations, and HUD
space.li4: Leaderboard, position tracking and real-time ranking display
space.li6: Game flow from lobby to in-game
space.li8: Scene lighting (point & global) and volume-based Post-Processing
space.p4: Applied vector math, calculus, and easing functions to achieve natural-feeling object movement and effects throughout the game. Getting the spaceship to feel responsive yet weighty in zero-gravity required lots of tuning and testing. I think I tuned the movement until the very last moment, right before the final presentation.
space.p5: Explored the fundamentals of networked games. Mainly, how client and server communicate state, the struggles of latency and synchronization, and the trade-offs between authoritative and client-predicted models. Even in a small project like this, designing systems that could function correctly in a multiplayer context taught me how games handle real-time data exchange.

soul.p1: This was my very first game. In fact, it was my first time doing anything really. Coding, Unity, game design... What an experience this project was.
soul.p2: Looking back, I would not say I learned a whole lot about programming from this project. It was all entry level knowledge about game development and programming, like movement, camera, interactions, and vector math. Overall, this project helped me build a solid foundation in Unity and C#. This introductory project showed me what game development is like and how to work with a team.
soul.p3: Also, it was a great learning experience for me to understand what it takes to ship a game from start to finish, and made me realize how much I am lacking in the technical side of things.
soul.li2: Progression System (We called it Quest System)
soul.p4: Hmm... Literally everything was a new challenge for me as I had 0 game dev knowledge prior to this project. Even using an IDE was a challenge for me at the time. It was one hell of a learning experience.
soul.p5: Few specific challenges I remember were creating the progression system and customizing the Dialogue System.
